props.title: Hud

sections.content: Hud (1963) revolutionized the American Western by stripping away romantic myths of the frontier. Paul Newman's portrayal of the amoral, selfish Hud Bannon directly challenged Hollywood's typical heroic cowboy archetype established in films like The Searchers (1956) and Shane (1953). Director Martin Ritt and cinematographer James Wong Howe used stark black-and-white photography to create a harsh, modern Texas landscape that reflected the moral decay at the story's center. The film's exploration of generational conflict between Hud and his principled father Homer parallels similar family dramas like East of Eden (1955), but with a darker, more cynical edge.

sections.content: The film's influence on "revisionist Westerns" cannot be overstated. Hud paved the way for morally ambiguous anti-heroes in films like The Wild Bunch (1969) and McCabe & Mrs. Miller (1971). Patricia Neal's Oscar-winning performance as Alma Brown brought unprecedented complexity to a female character in a Western, influencing later roles in films like Cat Ballou (1965) and The Quick and the Dead (1995). SUBHEAD: The Modern Anti-Hero Legacy

Newman's portrayal of Hud Bannon established a template for the charismatic villain-protagonist that resonated through subsequent decades. Films like Cool Hand Luke (1967) and Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969) built on this foundation, while modern works like There Will Be Blood (2007) and No Country for Old Men (2007) continue exploring similar themes of moral corruption in the American West. The film's unflinching look at environmental issues - through its cattle disease subplot - also presaged later eco-conscious Westerns like Dances with Wolves (1990).
